tagline.text: A small island in Southern Leyte, remembered as the setting of the Philippines' first Mass in 1521

location.label: Location
location.text: Limasawa, Southern Leyte (at the mouth of Sogod Bay, off Padre Burgos)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2 days, 1 night (a day trip is possible but tight)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~4,000 (2 days, 1 night, excluding round-trip flights from Manila)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) or Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport, Tacloban (TAC)

children.text: Limasawa is a small island municipality of about 7 km² at the southern tip of Southern Leyte, where the Magellan expedition is said to have held its Easter Mass in 1521. In a day or two you can see the First Mass shrine, the hilltop cross, the lighthouse and quiet beaches.
Limasawa is a small island south of Leyte, at the mouth of Sogod Bay where it meets the Bohol Sea. It is about
10km

long from north to south and covers roughly 6.98 km², making it the smallest municipality in Southern Leyte by both area and population. It has six barangays (Cabulihan, Lugsongan, Magallanes (Poblacion), San Agustin, San Bernardo and Trianas), and the 2024 census counted about 6,480 residents. Its nickname is "The First Mass Site in the Philippines."

The island is known because of what was recorded in 1521. Antonio Pigafetta, the chronicler of the Magellan expedition, called the island "Mazaua" and wrote that on March 28 the fleet met Rajah Colambu and Rajah Siaui of Butuan here. On Easter Sunday, March 31 of that year, Father Pedro de Valderrama is said to have celebrated the first Mass on Philippine soil, and Magellan climbed to the island's highest point, planted a cross and then left for Cebu. Exactly where Mazaua was has been debated by historians for a long time, but this island is known as the site the nation commemorates as the place of the First Mass.

Administratively, the island was separated from Padre Burgos by Presidential Decree No. 1549 on June 11, 1978, and became a full municipality after a plebiscite on August 27, 1989. It is a small, low-lying island, but its hills offer several viewpoints. Annual rainfall is about 1,326 mm, with April the driest month and November the wettest.

For travelers, Limasawa is a place for walking slowly rather than ticking off sights. There are no large resorts or shopping areas, only the road around the island, a few beaches and the monuments on the hill. In return you get a quiet atmosphere far from the bustle of Manila or Cebu. The trip involves several transfers and the boats run only about twice a day, so the best way to enjoy the island is to keep your schedule relaxed.

The First Mass shrine stands on a hill in Magallanes village. It is simply arranged, without elaborate decoration, and looks out over the sea. It commemorates the Mass of Easter, March 31, 1521, and pilgrims may arrive in large numbers around the anniversary event at the end of March each year.

A cross presented as Magellan's Cross stands on a hill with good views. One guide describes a short hike up a concrete staircase, while another puts the number of steps at about 450, so bring comfortable shoes and water. On clear days you can reportedly see the sea toward Bohol and Camiguin.

There is an old lighthouse at the tip of the island. From the end of the path leading up to it you can see the sea and the sunset. Near the southern end of the island there is also a small guesthouse called South Parola.

Dakdak Beach in Lugsongan village is described as having fine sand and calm water, suitable for swimming, picnics and camping. A resort of the same name offers overnight stays. The reef lies close to the shore, which makes snorkeling easy.

blocks.title: Island Lagoon and the coastal cliffs

children.text: A place called Island Lagoon has a small resort of the same name, and visitors report enjoying the water near the coastal cliffs. The path down to the shore is steep, so take care with children and older travelers.
The reef is close to the shore, so a mask and snorkel are enough to see underwater. Some guides mention gear rental of about
, so bring your own equipment if possible. Visibility varies a lot with the weather, so ask your boatman about conditions that day.

blocks.title: Village walks and an island tour

children.text: Walking through villages such as Trianas and Magallanes, you will see fish drying, small shops, schools and churches. items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: Cross on the morning boat and return on the afternoon boat

children.text: Take the morning boat from Padre Burgos.
Rent a habal-habal and visit the First Mass shrine and the cross on the hill.
Have a lunch of grilled fish at a local eatery.
Rest briefly on the beach, then return to the pier.
Take the afternoon boat back to the mainland.
On a day trip, bad weather or boat problems can make you miss the return boat. Leave some slack in your plans.

, and overnight ordinary ferries also run. One guide lists the one-way fare at about
From Maasin to Padre Burgos, travel by multicab or van. Schedules and fares change from year to year, so check the shipping line's latest announcements.
The outrigger boat from the Padre Burgos pier to Limasawa takes about
45 minutes to 1 hour
. Per 2026 guides the larger boat costs ₱100~150 one way (small bangkas ₱200~250), while 2025 guides list ₱70~120, so about

Even 2026 guides give different departure times (8:30, 10:30 and 11 AM, noon, 3 PM and 4 PM), and small boats leave once full. Service runs Monday to Saturday; on Sundays guides say there is no fixed schedule or no service, so check at the pier the day before. Boats back to the mainland mostly leave early in the morning, and one guide lists 1 PM as the last one.
If you miss the boat, you can find a small private boat. One guide lists about
for the whole boat.
Boats do not sail in bad weather. During the rainy season from June to October, leave spare days.
The main means of transport on the island are habal-habal (motorcycle taxis) and tricycles. Guides price an island tour per person or per vehicle for the day, at about
Because boats run only about twice a day and depend on sea conditions, the best time is
February–May

when the waves are calm. Clear skies also give good views from the hill and at sunset. April is the driest month, and around Easter at the end of March, commemorative events for the First Mass attract pilgrims.
During
June–November
rain is frequent, and typhoons and monsoon winds can cancel boats. November is known as the wettest month of the year. If you travel then, leave at least one spare day.

There are only a few places to stay. Guides often mention Dakdak Beach Resort (Lugsongan), Evashore Beach Resort (Magallanes), Island Lagoon Resort (San Agustin) and Trimulco Travelers Lodge (near the pier). Rates differ by guide: Trimulco lodge is listed at ₱400~500 in one guide but ₱1,200 in a 2026 visit report, a South Parola kubo room is about ₱800, Island Lagoon runs ₱1,000 (fan) to ₱1,500 (air-con), and Dakdak and Evashore air-conditioned rooms are ₱1,500~2,500. Confirm locally. Island Lagoon Resort has many steep steps down to the shore, so check if you are traveling with children or older relatives. Book ahead as soon as your dates are set.
Meals are mostly charcoal-grilled fish with rice and vegetables, along with sweet snacks made from coconut, cassava or sticky rice. Guides put a village eatery meal at about
and a resort meal at about
. Island shops have limited stock and tap water may not be drinkable, so buy bottled water and snacks in Maasin or Padre Burgos.
There are no ATMs. Withdraw all the cash you need for lodging, meals and tours in Maasin or Tacloban.
Boat times differ greatly between guides, so always confirm them at the Padre Burgos pier or your lodging the day before. It is safest to sleep on the mainland and take the first boat.
Power can go out on the island, so bring a power bank, and a phone that supports 4G/LTE works best.
The path to the cross has little shade. Climb early in the morning or toward evening and bring water and a hat.
The villages and the shrine are places of faith for local residents. Dress modestly and take your trash with you.
Talking first with the local tourism office or your boatman about guides and environmental fees helps avoid unnecessary disputes.
Bring snorkeling gear, sunscreen and a waterproof bag.
Around the March 31 First Mass anniversary the pier and lodging can be crowded. If pilgrimage is not your purpose, February or late April is more relaxed.
Boat times and fares differ between sources and boats are canceled in bad weather. Always confirm at the pier the day before departure and plan so you do not miss the return boat.
There are no ATMs on the island, and most lodging accepts cash only.
On days with typhoons or monsoon winds, boats do not sail and you may not be able to return to the mainland.
The interpretation of history (where Mazaua was) is a debated subject. Respect the signs and explanations you find on site.
Take care of slipping and falls when walking near hills and coastal cliffs.
Supplies on the island are limited. Bring medicine and personal items with you.
